### Reviewer 1

In this work, the authors, identify Claudin10 B as an important regulator of paracellular sodium transport in the ascending
thin limb of Henley. Using a Prox1-CE mouse, they discover that it can immediate recombination in the ATL and using a
sparse labeling strategy discover that ATL epithelia are characterized by interdigitating finger like protrusions. Using single
nucleus RNA-seq they identify Claudin 10 as a marker of a TL and show that it is enriched at the cell membrane of the ATL.
Using an in vitro model they demonstrate that Claudin10B is sufficient to drive membrane waviness, a surrogate for these
finger like protrusion. They generate a Claudin10B knockout in the ATL and show that Claudin10B is required for urinary
concentration. Finally, they perform structure function studies and confirm that Claudin10b interacts with Zo1 to drive these
membrane in interdigitation and regulate urine osmolarity.
Overall, this is a highly novel work that reveals in unexpected epithelial morphology, and provides strong evidence that
Claudin10b is required for urinary concentration.
1. Can the authors directly measure paracellular sodium transport using their qKO MDCKII model, perhaps by TEER, to
directly probe the role of Claudin10b, ZO1 and membrane ruffling in sodium transport?

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript characterizes the morphology and functional elements of the aTL, which is a poorly understood segment of
the nephron. This is an important advance in our knowledge of renal physiology, which is key for better understanding fluid
and electrolyte disorders, and potentially even for developing new medications, such as diuretics. The study also offers a
new method for specific genetic targeting of the aTL, which will serve as an important tool for further investigations of this
nephron segment.
The work is original and significant, as it elucidates the previously undescribed morphology of aTL cells while providing a
mechanism for the functional significance of the morphology. The focal point of the study, Claudin-10b, is also expressed in
the TAL, and there is a study by Quintanova et al that describes the role of Claudin-10b in producing a similar morphology of
membrane infoldings or protrusions in TAL cells – the authors briefly allude to this feature of Claudin-10b and cite the
Quintanova et al manuscript in the discussion, but they could spend a little more time describing the similarities and
differences between the role of Claudin-10b in TAL vs aTL morphologies.
The work does support the conclusion that Claudin-10b is required for normal aTL morphology. However, a few clarifications
are needed.
1. In the abstract, the authors state that Claudin-10b “proves both necessary and sufficient” for interdigitation formation –
while they show that it is necessary, they have not provided adequate evidence to claim that it is “sufficient”. In fact, they
show that ZO-1 is required for formation of the protrusions in aTL cells – so Claudin-10b is not sufficient. They also perhaps
make this claim because Claudin-10b can restore membrane waviness in MDCK cells that lack expression of other claudins
– however, this is an artificial in vitro system that is a tool to study Claudin-10b function but cannot faithfully recapitulate aTL
morphology and function. The ability of Claudin-10b to restore membrane waviness in MDCK cells, therefore, does not
necessarily indicate that it is sufficient for protrusion formation in aTL cells.
2. In the first section of the results, the authors should clearly state that Prox1 expression is very specific to the TAL and aTL
and is not expressed in other parts of the inner medulla (namely, descending thin limb and inner medullary collecting duct)
as shown by Kim et al. (the paper cited by the authors) – this will just help highlight the specificity of their Cre recombinase.
3. In the results section titled “Caludin-10b is the aTL isoform”, the authors state “since no other tubules in the inner medulla
expressed claudin-10” – is this claim based on their single nucleus RNA sequencing data?
4. Why is apical-junctional membrane “waviness” or “ruffling” a good surrogate for lateral protrusion formation? Is it just
because of the morphological similarity? It would be good to also show some molecular similarities that justify this as a
surrogate for aTL protrusions.
5. Why does the induction of Prox1-creERT2 at different time points lead to recombination only in aTL vs TAL? Is Prox1
expressed in the aTL earlier than in TAL? Is there evidence of this?
6. Were the 24 hour urine osmolality and urine volume studies done in Cldn10 cKO mice where induction of Cre expression
was limited to aTL by Tamoxifen-mediated induction between P2-P7? This is important to clarify, because of course the
Cldn10 cKO where Cre expression is induced at an older age to target both the aTL and TAL will not be able to differentiate
between the effect of aTL vs TAL on urinary concentrating ability. Maybe the Cldn10 cKO specific to aTL and not TAL can be
re-named to stress the difference if the studies were done in the aTL-specific Cldn10
cKO. If the studies were done in the
older cKO, then they need to be releated in the aTL-specific cKO.
7. In the last section of the results, it would be good to show whether ZO1 or ZO2 or both colocalize with Claudin-10b in the
aTL – these studies are all in vitro in MDCK, which helps shed some mechanistic insights on how Claudin-10b interacts with
other tight junction proteins, but again, it’s not a faithful representation of how Claudin-10b actually behaves in the aTL. This
is obviously very difficult to replicate in vitro because no kidney cells will behave the same outside the kidney, but some high
resolution co-staining with ZO1 and ZO2 could help strengthen the in vitro findings.
8. In the discussion, the authors claim that “this finding resolves a decades-old question by establishing that the inner
medulla actively participates in urine concentration, rather than merely serving as a passive conduit for osmotic
equilibration.” This is an inaccurate statement – Claudin-10b is a cation channel that facilitates passive diffusion of cations
but not an active transporter like NKCC2 in the TAL.

### Reviewer 3

This study offers a straightforward and rather elegant explanation for how mammals generate highly concentrated urine for
organismal fluid balance.
Data summary: The ascending thin limb (aTL) of the nephron is long known to reside in the inner medulla, which manifests
the highest osmolality in the kidney. This study validated nephron segment-“quasi-specific” genetic lineage labeling tools to
address this question, using the Prox1-CreERT2mTmG reporter. Induction with dilute Tamoxifen concentrations allowed
visualization of lineage labeled single cell features with unprecedented clarity, revealing time-dependent development
(weeks-months) of highly branched, membrane interdigitations, resulting in a ‘sunburst-like’ cell presumably suited for ion-
transport function, given the expanded junctional seam area for these cells (Fig. 1). To understand genes/protein that drive
this morphological transition, the authors carried out single nuclear transcriptomics across post-natal development (Fig. 2),
identifying top differentially expressed genes for the aTL cluster, settling on Claudin 10 as a gene that emerges during the
temporal window when membrane interdigitation develops (Fig. 2D,E). Since Claudin 10 comes in two functionally distinct
isoforms (A,B), the authors showed it was the cation-specific 10b isoform that is expressed the aTL (Fig. 2G), consistent with
it being a candidate for sodium resorption in the kidney.
The authors turned to a reductionist claudin-null MDCK cell system to address whether Cldn10b was sufficient to drive
similar apical junction features seen in the aTL (Fig. 3; Fig. S5). MDCK tight junctions are known to display waviness in
mature monolayers, a feature previously ascribed to the claudins expressed in MDCK. Using this system, the authors
showed that Cldn10b is sufficient (in the MDCK-pan claudin-null background) to promote apical junction waviness, using
established calculation methods. Most remarkably, targeted loss of Claudin10 in mice inhibited the apical junction
waviness/interdigitation in aTL cells (Fig. 3C-F). Along with these dramatic morphological differences, the authors show
functional differences in urine osmolarity—where the Cldn10 KO mice show more dilute urine, suggestive of less capacity to
resorb sodium (Fig. 4). To further refine understanding- the authors use a panel of previously established mutants, to show
that it is the transcellular-recognition and ZO-1/ZO-2-binding domains of Cldn10, but not its ion-selective function, that is
required for the wavy/interdigitated morphology (Fig. 5).
Assessment: Overall, this is a clearly presented well designed study that links a spectacular aTL apical junction/membrane
form to kidney function/generation of concentrated urine. The notion that Cldns are regulators of epithelial membrane
structure- not simply barrier function as previously known, is compelling. I have no major concerns, but have technical
questions and minor suggestions regarding terminology (e.g., ruffling, protrusions, lateral interdigitations), which may better
align with terminology in the epithelial junction field.
Major Questions:
1. Is it possible that the Cldn10 KO alters the time dependence of the membrane elaborations, but does not completely block
it? How long out were cell phenotypes characterized in the KO condition? Is it possible that the Cldn10 KO merely delays,
rather that fully blocks the membrane elaborations? Please elaborate.
2. Is there an overall viability phenotype with the Prox-Cldn10 KO mouse?
3. For the urine osmolarity measurements in Fig. 4, did the authors use the lowest dose of TMX to bias Cldn10 removal from
the medulla, rather than other segments of the nephron?
Minor:
1. Lines 9; 97; Line 297: The authors often refer to the apical junction membrane interdigitations as ‘lateral’ interdigitations. I
think this could be confusing. Lateral interdigitations have been described in MDCK (PMID: 34099568), which are much
taller than the 1um-thin aTL cells (Fig S1). I might refer to these as apical junction interdigitations for better alignment with
work of others in MDCK (PMID: 35389423), and in distinction from true basolateral invaginations (PMID: 34099568).
Alternatively, if Cldn10b really drives lateral interdigitations as well- please show full x-z stacks for images in Fig 5D and F
(comparing the Cldn10b WT vs PDZ-binding motif mutant as control) to show that this is really a lateral interdigitation, as in
PMID: 34099568. Also, I might not refer to the MDCK apical waviness as “membrane ruffling” (line 162), as that term is often
used to describe a behavior of the true apical membrane (not the apical junction), as in a recent study that generates these
ruffles to release membrane tension and favor micropinocytosis (PMID: 40550809).
2. It does seem that claudin 10 is not very co-local with ZO-1 in the MDCK cell system (Fig. 5D), but rather more basolateral
to ZO-1. This somewhat undercuts the suggestion that the apical junction/waviness phenotype is due to a
constitutive/stoichiometric interaction between Cldn10b/ZO-1, perhaps favoring a more indirect mechanism?
3. Figure 1G shows a very nice time course of aTL morphological development. Based on this sequence, and absent live
imaging- I might not refer to these structures as “protrusions”- since protrusive behavior is not yet known. Indeed, given top
gene in Fig. 2D indicates high expression of an actin severing component- the morphological changes that occur slowly
between post-natal day 14 and 6 weeks might be through some sort of membrane retraction/sculpting mechanism. This is a
minor quibble, but it is probably best to use a term that is mechanistically agnostic to how the structures are ultimately
generated. Finger-like ‘projections” might be better.
4. “ultrastructural analysis” (line 70) historically refers to analysis at the EM level, not light microscopic level.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Mammals achieve the highest urine concentrations of any vertebrate, a feat that hinges on generating steep osmotic gradients within the renal medulla. Interestingly, the region with the highest osmolality, the inner medulla, is unique to mammals. Among the nephron’s segments, the ascending thin limb (aTL) is the sole element exclusive to this zone and is thought to mediate passive salt reabsorption. However, the architecture and functional impact of the aTL have remained obscure. Here we uncover an unexpected morphogenetic program in the aTL, characterized by extensive apical-junctional interdigitations that greatly increase cell-to-cell contact area. Integrating single-nucleus transcriptomics with high-resolution imaging, we identify claudin-10b, a tight junction protein and paracellular cation pore, as a central driver of this architecture. Inducible deletion of claudin-10b specifically in the aTL abolishes membrane interdigitations and markedly reduces urine-concentrating ability, thereby establishing a direct link between segment-specific epithelial morphology and whole-organ function. Claudin-10b proves necessary for interdigitation formation, acting through transcellular adhesion and interaction with the tight-junction scaffold ZO1. These findings offer definitive evidence that the inner medulla and aTL are essential for maximal urinary concentration, while revealing a non-canonical, morphogenetic role for claudin-10b.

---

## Introduction

The ability to concentrate urine represents one of the most remarkable physiological adaptations in mammalian evolution, enabling survival in terrestrial environments by conserving water while eliminating metabolic waste. This critical function depends on the kidney's capacity to establish and maintain steep osmotic gradients across the renal medulla, with the inner medulla, a specialized compartment unique to mammals, acting as a primary site for achieving maximal urine concentration1,2.

The nephron, the functional unit of the kidney, comprises a series of morphologically and functionally distinct segments that collectively fine-tune solute and water balance. Among these segments, the Loop of Henle (LOH) plays a pivotal role in establishing the corticomedullary osmotic gradient essential for urine concentration (Fig. 1a)2. The thick ascending limb (TAL) in the outer medulla is well-characterized for its active sodium chloride transport, which drives the initial establishment of medullary hypertonicity3,4. In contrast, the inner medullary thin segments operate primarily through passive transport mechanisms, as ATP-driven active transport systems are notably absent in this region5,6.

Within the inner medulla, the ascending thin limb (aTL) of the Loop of Henle stands as the sole nephron segment confined exclusively to this region1. Despite its unique position and presumed role in passive salt reabsorption, the aTL has remained one of the most enigmatic components of renal physiology since Kokko and Rector first proposed passive inner medullary sodium reabsorption in the 1970s7. While chloride transport in the aTL has been demonstrated to occur transcellularly via the chloride channel Clck18-10, the molecular mechanisms governing sodium transport remain poorly understood5,6. The aTL's deep anatomical location within the inner medulla, combined with the historical lack of segment-specific genetic tools11, has severely hampered mechanistic studies of this critical nephron segment. These technical limitations have left fundamental questions unanswered regarding the precise molecular mechanisms underlying aTL function, its contribution to medullary hypertonicity, and the structural features that enable its physiological role.

Here, we report the presence of a unique epithelial architecture in the aTL: extensive apical-junctional membrane interdigitations that dramatically expand cell-to-cell contact area. Through integration of single-nucleus transcriptomics, high-resolution imaging, and functional studies, we identify claudin-10b as a central molecular driver of this unique morphology. We demonstrate that claudin-10b functions through transcellular adhesive interactions and tight junction scaffolding proteins to create these interdigitations, and that this architectural program is essential for normal urinary concentrating ability. Our findings establish direct evidence for aTL-specific contributions to kidney function while definitively demonstrating an in vivo morphogenetic role for claudin proteins that extends beyond their traditional functions in epithelial barrier formation.

## Results

Identification of arborized aTL projections
To identify molecular mechanisms underlying inner medullary urine concentration, we focused on the ascending thin limb (aTL) of the Loop of Henle. Previous studies reported expression of Prox1, a transcription factor known as a master regulator of lymphatic development12, in the developing aTL13. Based on this, we hypothesized that the Prox1-CreERT2 knock-in mouse could be used as a genetic entry point to target this nephron segment. To test this, we crossed Prox1-CreERT2 knock-in mice14 with the mTmG reporter line and induced recombination at 4 weeks of age. With mTmG, cells express membrane-tdTomato (mT) before Cre recombination and membrane-GFP (mG) after. We observed a strong GFP signal in the inner medulla, a region that lacks lymphatic vessels (Fig. 1b). Co-localization of the medullary GFP signal with the chloride channel Clck1/2, a marker of the ascending LOH11,15, established that Prox1-CreERT2 drives recombination in the aTL and thick ascending limb (TAL) (Fig. 1b,c). Adjacent medullary tubules, including the collecting duct, the descending thin limb, and the vasculature, do not express Prox1 (Supplementary Fig. 1).

A low dose of tamoxifen administered to Prox1-CreERT2; mTmG mice resulted in sparse GFP labeling of the aTL and TAL (Fig. 1d), which enabled visualization of single aTL cells. Surprisingly, this revealed a striking sunburst morphology characterized by interdigitating, finger-like cell projections that extend laterally between adjacent cells rather than apically like microvilli (Fig. 1d, Supplementary Movies 1-3). Three-dimensional reconstructions of individuals cells via confocal microscopy (Fig. 1e) and Axially-Swept Light-sheet Microscopy (ASLM)16 (Fig. 1f, Supplementary Movie 4) further resolved these projections into high-curvature primary processes with branched secondary processes.

The aTL projections developed postnatally, increasing in number and length from postnatal day 7 (P7) until adulthood (Fig. 1g). Structural analysis revealed that they contained a cortical actin network, microtubules, and mitochondria, supporting their identity as cytoplasmic extensions (Supplementary Fig. 2). Filamentous actin was most enriched at the junctional regions, aligning parallel to the plasma membrane, rather than as a core actin bundle (Supplementary Fig. 2a,b). The discovery of these elaborate projections raised fundamental questions about the molecular mechanisms governing cell morphology, particularly the drivers of interdigitations in the aTL.

Claudin-10 in the developing aTL
To investigate how aTL cells form these interdigitating projections, we conducted a time-course single nucleus (snuc) RNA sequencing experiment at postnatal day 0 (P0), P2, P7, P14, P21 and 6 weeks, capturing the transcriptional landscape of postnatal projection development. At 6 weeks, we identified a distinct aTL cluster that expressed Prox1 and Clck1 but lacked markers of other nephron segments, such as Slc12a1 (NKCC2), a TAL marker (Fig. 2a,b, Supplementary Fig. 3). The identity of the aTL cluster was further validated by demonstrating that Prox1-CreERT2; mTmG GFP signal in the inner medulla colocalized with aTL markers (Prox1, Clck1) (Fig. 2c) but did not overlap with markers of near-by nephron segments (Supplementary Fig. 1b,c). This confirmed that the aTL cluster identified by snucRNA-sequencing corresponds to a distinct Prox1+ epithelial population in the inner medulla.

To uncover molecular regulators of aTL morphology, we performed differential gene expression analysis within the aTL cluster. One intriguing candidate was Cldn10, which encodes the transmembrane tight junction protein claudin-10 (Fig. 2d). Although also expressed in the proximal tubule and TAL (Supplementary Fig. 4a, Supplementary Movies 5-6), Cldn10 was among the top twenty enriched genes in aTL (13th overall) (Fig. 2d). Importantly, Cldn10 transcript levels increased postnatally, coinciding with the emergence of aTL projections (Fig. 2e, 1g). Claudin-10 has been shown to immunolocalize to the aTL17, and was the most highly expressed claudin in the aTL, surpassing others by at least threefold (Supplementary Fig. 4b). Its enrichment in the aTL was corroborated by an independent mouse kidney dataset18, and Cldn10 has been identified as a marker gene in human aTL19.

Immunostaining confirmed that claudin-10 colocalized with the mosaic Prox1-CreERT2; mTmG GFP signal in the inner medulla, specifically at sites of interdigitation along the periphery of aTL projections (Fig. 2f). At the subcellular level, claudin-10 predominantly localized to apical junctions, colocalizing with its interactors ZO1 and ZO2 (Supplementary Fig. 5)20,21.

Claudin-10b is the aTL isoform
Claudin-10 exists as two isoforms, claudin-10a and claudin-10b, which differ only in their first exon, but exhibit distinct functions: claudin-10a forms anion pores, while claudin-10b forms cation pores22,23. To identify which isoform is expressed in the aTL, we performed RT-PCR on RNA isolated from the cortex, outer medulla and inner medulla. As expected, claudin-10a was detected in the cortex, while claudin-10b was expressed in the outer medulla (Fig. 2g), consistent with its known localization in the proximal tubule and TAL, respectively22,23. In the inner medulla, claudin-10b was the isoform detected (Fig. 2g). Notably, since no other tubules in the inner medulla expressed claudin-10 (Supplementary Fig. 4c), these findings confirm that the aTL produces claudin-10b, expanding its known expression profile to this nephron segment.

Claudin-10b regulates epithelial morphology
To investigate the role of claudin-10b in cell morphology, we first turned to an in vitro system amenable to mechanistic analysis. Notably, no existing epithelial cell culture model fully recapitulates the complex interdigitating projections observed in the aTL. However, a related feature, apical-junctional membrane ‘waviness’ can serve as a mechanistically relevant readout for apical-junctional interdigitations.

MDCKII cells, a widely used kidney epithelial cell line, exhibit modest junctional membrane waviness24,25, making them a suitable system in which both gain- and loss-of-function effects on junctional morphology can be readily detected. Importantly, while wild-type MDCKII cells express multiple claudins, including claudin-1, -2, -3, -4, and -7, previous studies have shown that simultaneous knockout of these five major claudins (quinKO or qKO) eliminates membrane waviness24,26.

Strikingly, we found that claudin-10b expression in quinKO cells induced pronounced apical-junctional membrane waviness (Fig. 3a). This phenotype was quantified using an automated ‘waviness index’, a metric comparing the convex hull perimeter to the actual plasma membrane perimeter (Fig. 3b, Supplementary Fig. 6), with higher values indicating increased membrane waviness (see Methods for additional details). Automated measurements correlated well with a manual measure of membrane waviness, underscoring the robustness and reliability of this approach. In addition to its effects on junctional morphology, claudin-10b expression increased transepithelial resistance, decreased conductance, and increased paracellular sodium selectivity in quinKO cells, as assessed by PNa/PCl ratios and dilution potentials (Supplementary Fig. S7), consistent with previous reports24,26.

A dual role for claudin-10b in aTL structure and function in vivo
While our in vitro findings demonstrated that claudin-10b promotes apical-junctional membrane waviness, it remained unclear whether claudin-10b similarly regulates epithelial morphology in vivo, where aTL cells form elaborate interdigitations. In addition, the functional role of claudin-10b in aTL physiology remained unclear. Given claudin-10b’s localization at aTL interdigitations and its function as a paracellular cation pore, we hypothesized that claudin-10b has dual roles: regulating epithelial morphology via interdigitations and contributing to urinary concentrating ability, potentially by influencing sodium handling.

To evaluate the role of claudin-10b in the aTL, we generated a conditional knockout mouse by flanking exons 2 and 3 of Cldn10 with loxP sites (Supplementary Fig. 8). Cldn10f/+ mice were crossed with Cldn10f/+;Prox1-CreERT2; mTmG mice to produce control (Cldn10+/+;Prox1-CreERT2; mTmG) and mutant (Cldn10f/f;Prox1-CreERT2; mTmG) mice, ensuring that both groups carried a fluorescent reporter to visualize aTL projections. Cldn10 mutant mice were healthy, with no differences in weight between genotypes at 10 weeks of age (mean ± SD : CTL, 20.17 ± 3.31g [n=18]; HET, 20.60 ± 2.17g [n=15]; MUT, 20.71 ± 3.85g [n=17]; Kruskal-Wallis Test, p>0.99 for all comparisons).

Immunofluorescence confirmed that recombined GFP+ tubules in Cldn10 mutant mice lacked claudin-10 protein (Fig. 3c,d). Notably, Cldn10 mutant mice displayed a drastic reduction in aTL cell projections, with many cells completely lacking interdigitations. (Fig. 3e). Although plasma membrane surface area was greatly reduced from the lack of interdigitations, the tight junction adaptor protein ZO1 was still appropriately recruited to the plasma membrane at levels comparable to controls (Fig. 3f,g).

The physiologic function of the aTL is poorly understood, particularly its contribution to solute transport and urine concentration. Although the aTL has been implicated in passive sodium and chloride reclamation5,6, its definitive contribution to medullary hypertonicity, which is essential for urine concentration, has not been established. Moreover, the molecular mechanisms governing sodium movement in the aTL remain unresolved. A major barrier to testing claudin-10b’s role in this segment has been the lack of genetic tools capable of selectively manipulating the aTL in vivo. Our discovery that Prox1-CreERT2 induces recombination in the aTL and TAL provided a promising genetic tool, but achieving aTL specificity required further refinement. Single nucleus transcriptomic analysis revealed that Prox1 is expressed in the developing aTL prior to the TAL (Supplementary Fig. 9), with expression in both segments at later developmental timepoints (Supplementary Fig. 9). Consistent with this pattern, neonatal tamoxifen administration from postnatal day 2 (P2) to P7 selectively targeted the aTL (Supplementary Fig. 10a-c), whereas tamoxifen administered at later timepoints resulted in recombination in both the aTL and the TAL (Supplementary Fig. 10d-i). This temporal control of Prox1-CreERT2 therefore enabled genetic analysis of aTL-specific gene function. Claudin-10 is absent from renal lymphatics at all tamoxifen dosing ages analyzed (Supplementary Fig. 11), indicating the observed phenotype is unlikely to arise from lymphatic recombination.

To assess the functional consequences of Cldn10 loss specifically within the aTL, we administered the aTL-selective tamoxifen regimen (P2-P7, hereafter referred to as Cldn10ΔaTL) to control (CTL), heterozygous (HET), and Cldn10 mutant (MUT) mice. Under baseline conditions, Cldn10ΔaTL mutant mice exhibited reduced urine osmolality and increased 24-hour urine volume compared with controls (Fig. 4a,b). To determine if these changes reflected a defect in urinary concentrating ability rather than increased water intake, we subjected mice to 24-hour water deprivation. Under these conditions, urine osmolality increased in all groups; however, Cldn10ΔaTL mutants achieved a significantly lower maximal urine osmolality than control and heterozygous littermates (Fig. 4c; Supplementary Fig. 12). These findings indicate a reduced maximal concentrating capacity after aTL-specific deletion of Cldn10.

Notably, non-recombined aTL cells in mutant mice that were not adjacent to recombined cells exhibited normal projections, indicating that the phenotype is primarily cell-autonomous rather than driven by local osmotic or other microenvironmental changes (Supplementary Fig. 13).

Claudin-10 transcellular adhesion drives projections
While our in vivo findings demonstrated that claudin-10b is essential for aTL projection formation, the molecular mechanism by which claudin-10b promotes membrane interdigitation remained unclear. To address this, we conducted in vitro mutagenesis targeting key functional domains of claudin-10b.

Claudin-10b contains two extracellular loops (ECL1 and ECL2)27, where ECL1 governs sodium permeability, and ECL2 mediates transcellular adhesive interactions (Fig. 5a)28. To dissect the relative contributions of sodium transport and cell-cell adhesion to projection formation, we generated point mutants in ECL1 (D65N) and ECL2 (F146A), both of which have been previously validated and characterized29-31.

Strikingly, expression of the claudin-10b D65N mutant, which disrupts sodium permeability while preserving adhesive interactions, induced apical-junctional projections. In contrast, expression of the claudin-10b F146A mutant, which disrupts transcellular adhesion, failed to induce projections (Fig. 5b,c). These findings suggest that transcellular adhesive interactions, rather than paracellular sodium transport, are critical for interdigitation.

To directly test whether transcellular interactions between neighboring cells are required for interdigitations, we co-cultured quinKO cells with quinKO+Cldn10b-expressing cells and examined the clonal interface (Fig. 5d). Notably, projections were absent at this boundary, despite robust projection formation between adjacent claudin-10b-expressing cells, providing direct evidence that transcellular adhesion is required for claudin-10b-mediated interdigitation.

Based on this observation, we re-examined mutant epithelia in vivo to identify aTL sections with mosaic deletion of claudin-10. Consistent with our in vitro findings, non-recombined claudin-10-expressing cells adjacent to claudin-10-deficient cells failed to form projections (Fig. 5e). Together, these three lines of evidence strongly suggest that claudin-10’s adhesive transcellular interactions, rather than its role in sodium transport, are essential for epithelial interdigitation in the aTL.

Projections require claudin-10b-ZO1 binding
In quinKO+Cldn10b cells, we observed that claudin-10 localizes to both the apical junctions and the lateral membrane (Supplementary Fig. 14a), similarly to some other claudin family members in MDCK cells24,32,33. Notably, membrane waviness was confined to apical junctions where claudin-10 co-localized with ZO1, a tight junction adaptor protein previously shown to promote junctional membrane waviness when expressed at high levels34. Membrane waviness was not observed along lateral membranes lacking ZO1 (Supplementary Fig. 14a).

To determine whether interactions between claudin-10b and tight junction scaffold proteins are required for interdigitation, we expressed claudin-10ΔYV, a C-terminal mutant lacking the PDZ-binding motif necessary for ZO1/2 interaction21, in quinKO cells. In contrast to wild type claudin-10b, claudin-10ΔYV accumulated intracellularly rather than localizing to the plasma membrane and failed to induce membrane projections (Fig. 5f). This suggests that PDZ-mediated interactions are necessary for claudin-10b localization and function, but does not distinguish if ZO1/2 are the key factors.

To distinguish whether loss of projections reflected impaired membrane localization versus loss of scaffold interactions, we engineered claudin-10ΔYV-CAAX, a variant incorporating a CAAX motif to promote plasma membrane association35. Although this modification sporadically restored claudin-10b localization at the plasma membrane, only very slight membrane waviness was observed (Fig. 5f). This indicates that membrane localization of claudin-10ΔYV is not sufficient to rescue projection formation.

To determine whether ZO1 or ZO2 are specifically required for claudin-10b function, we generated single knockouts of ZO1 or ZO2 in quinKO+Cldn10b cells. Due to incomplete knockout efficiency, the resulting cultures contained a mixture of ZO1+ and ZO1– cells (Fig. 5g,h) or ZO2+ and ZO2– cells (Supplementary Fig. 14b), effectively creating co-cultures within individual wells. This enabled direct comparison of membrane morphology between knockout and wild-type cells in the same environment. Loss of either ZO1 or ZO2 did not impair recruitment of claudin-10b to the plasma membrane (Fig. 5g, Supplementary Fig. 14b) and neither knockout impacted the localization of the other (Fig. 5h, Supplementary Fig. 14b), consistent with previous reports34. However, ZO1– cells failed to form projections (Fig. 5g,h), indicating that ZO1 is required for claudin-10b-mediated morphogenesis. Notably, ZO1 was required in both cells for projections to form (Fig. 5g,h arrows).

Loss of ZO2 displayed an intermediate phenotype, with reduced but not absent projections (Supplementary Fig. 14b). These mechanistic insights likely also apply to the in vivo aTL tubule, where claudin-10 co-localizes with ZO1/2 (Supplementary Fig. 5). Together these findings support a model in which both claudin-10b transcellular interactions and claudin-10b-ZO1 interactions are required to drive apical-junctional membrane projections (Fig. 5i).

## Methods

All research in this study complies with ethical regulations and guidelines, including UT Southwestern IACUC.

Reagents: All reagents are listed in Supplementary Tables 1-3.

Animals
Mice were housed in a 12-hour light/dark cycle (6am - 6 pm) with the temperature held between 68-79˚F and humidity ranging between 30-70%. Mice were maintained on a mixed C57Bl6/129X1/SvJ genetic background and genotyped by standard PCR. See Supplementary Table 2 for primer information. Cldn10f/f were generated using EasiCrispr52 (Supplementary Fig. 8). Cldn10f/+ females were bred to Cldn10f/+;Prox1-CreERT2; mTmG14 males to obtain control (Cldn10+/+;Prox1-CreERT2; mTmG), heterozygous (Cldn10f/+;Prox1-CreERT2; mTmG), and mutant (Cldn10f/f;Prox1-CreERT2; mTmG) mice. 75 mg/kg tamoxifen was administered orally or via intraperitoneal injections at designated times. Further details are provided in Supplementary Fig. 10. All procedures followed UTSW IACUC-approved guidelines. Male and female mice were used for each experiment (see figure legend for details), and all observations reported are applicable to both sexes. The ages of animals used in each experiment are detailed in the figure legends.

RT-PCR
Cortex, outer medulla and inner medulla of 8-week-old mixed sex mice were dissected. RNA was isolated using the RNeasy Mini Kit and cDNA was synthesized using SuperScript III Reverse transcriptase. Primers sequences are available in Supplementary Table 223.

Single nucleus RNA sequencing
The kidney pairs of two male and two female mice at each age (P0, P2, P7, P14, P21, 6wk) were dissected in cold PBS. Cortical regions were partially removed to enrich for medullary cell types. Kidneys were minced into small cubes, dounced 5 times with the loose pestle in Nuclei Lysis Buffer 1 (NLB1) (4 ml of nuclei EZ lysis buffer, 20 µl of RNasin Plus, 20 µl of SUPERaseIN, 1% BSA, cOmplete ULTRA tablet), and passed through a 200 µm strainer. The sample was then dounced 10 times with the tight pestle, incubated for 1 minutes in NLB1 on ice, passed through a 40 µm strainer, and centrifuged at 500g for 1 minutes at 4˚C. The pellet was resuspended in NLB2 (4 ml of Nuclei EZ Lysis Buffer, 4 µl of RNasin Plus, 4 µl of SUPERaseIN, 1% BSA, cOmplete ULTRA tablet), incubated on ice for 5 minutes, and centrifuged at 500g for 5 minutes at 4˚C. The pellet was resuspended in nuceli suspension buffer (2 ml of calcium/magnesium free PBS, 2 µl of RNasin Plus, 2% BSA) and passed through a 5 µm strainer. The nuclei were counted by hemocytometer and diluted to 1200 nuclei/uL.

Libraries were prepared from 10,000 nuclei per timepoint using the 10x Genomics Chromium Next GEM Single Cell 3’ Kit v3.1 kit. All samples were sequenced on a NovaSeq S4 with 50,000 reads per cell and 28x90 read length.

Single-nucleus RNA-seq preprocessing
Filtered feature-barcode matrices were generating by running the CellRanger count pipeline. Nuclei were called from empty droplets by testing for deviation of the expression profile for each cell from the ambient RNA pool53. Nuclei with low numbers of detected genes or library sizes, as defined as a deviation greater than three median absolute deviations (MADs) below the median, were excluded from further analysis. Nuclei with large mitochondrial proportions, i.e., more than 3 mean-absolute deviations above the median, with a minimum difference between the threshold of 0.5% between the threshold for exclusion and the median mitochondrial transcript count, were removed. Nuclei were pre-clustered and a deconvolution method was applied to compute size factors for all cells54 and normalized log-expression values were calculated.

Single-nucleus RNA-seq analysis
Cells were clustered by building a shared nearest neighbor graph55 on the normalized expression data and executing the Louvain algorithm. Diffusion maps were calculated using an adaption of the algorithm presented in Haghverdi et al56. Normalized expression data was imputed applying Markov Affinity-based Graph Imputation of Cells (MAGIC)57 to the previously constructed diffusion maps. Marker genes for each subset of cells under investigation were calculated by applying the EIGEN algorithm58. Differential expression between pre-specified groups of nuclei was calculated from the Hurdle model implemented in the MAST59 Bioconductor package. Gene set enrichment analysis was performed for sets curated in MsigDb60 using with fgsea61 Bioconductor package. For each set, the enrichment in each cell was calculated using AUCell62. Normalized expression data and marker gene analysis (consensus markers) are available in Supplementary Data 1-7. Expression plots for genes of interest expression were generated using dplyr, tidyr, and ggplot2 packages in RStudio (Version 2025.05.1+513).

Cell culture
MDCKII cells (gift from Keith Mostov) were grown in 10% DMEM low glucose with 2 mM L-glutamine. Cells were grown in 8-well chamber slides and imaged using a Zeiss 880 confocal microscope63,64. Quintuple knockout (quinKO) MDCKII cells (gift from Mikio Furuse) were generated using TALEN vectors24. Wild-type and mutant Cldn10b constructs were synthesized, validated by Sanger sequencing, and cloned into pENTR221 by ThermoFisher GeneArt Services. These constructs were inserted into the inducible lentiviral vector pCW57.1 using Gateway cloning. ZO1 and ZO2 gRNAs65 were cloned into the pLV[2CRISPR]-hCas9:T2A:Bsd-U6 Dual gRNA lentiviral vector by VectorBuilder. ZO1 and ZO2 gRNAs are detailed in Supplementary Table 2. Lentiviruses were packaged in HEK293T (gift from Keith Mostov) using Mirus-TransIT-LT1, and viral supernatant was harvested for transduction after 48 hours. Transduced quinKO cells were selected with puromycin (5 µg/mL) for pCW57.1 or blasticidin (10 µg/mL) for ZO1/ZO2 knock-out. Heterogeneous or clonal populations were used for analysis as indicated. Inducible cell lines were treated with 0.5 to 10 µg/mL doxycycline as indicated for 4-5 days. For immunofluorescence, cells were plated at 6.6x104 cells/well in 8-well chamber slides and cultured for 5-7 days.

In vitro electrophysiology and measurement of dilution potentials
Cells were seeded onto 12 mm Snapwell inserts with a 0.4 µm pore polycarbonate membrane (Corning 3407) at a density of 1x105 and incubated for 7 days with media changes every other day. At 7 days post-seeding, inserts were mounted in modified Ussing chambers (P2300, Physiologic Instruments Inc., Venice, FL, U.S.A.) with an exposed surface area of 1.12 cm2 maintained at 37 °C under symmetrical, current-clamp conditions (VCC MC6; Physiologic Instruments) with Buffer A (120 mM NaCl, 5 mM KCl, 10 mM NaHCO3, 1.2 mM CaCl2, 1 mM MgSO4, 10 mM HEPES, and 10 mM glucose, pH 7.4), which was simultaneously gassed and stirred with 95% O2/5% CO2. Following a 20-minute equilibration, dilution potentials were determined by replacing Buffer A in the basolateral chamber with Buffer B (60 mM NaCl, 120 mM mannitol, 5 mM KCl, 10 mM NaHCO3, 1.2 mM CaCl2, 1 mM MgSO4, 10 mM HEPES, and 10 mM glucose, pH 7.4) and recording transepithelial voltage (Vt) for 5 minutes. Buffer B was then replaced with Buffer A and Vt recorded for a further 5 minutes. The Na+/Cl- permeability ratios (PNa/PCl) were calculated using the mean of the last twelve data points (one minute) recorded during a given measurement period following the buffer change66. Transepithelial resistance was calculated by Ohm’s Law using the deflection in Vt following the application of a 40 µA pulse at 5 second intervals. Electrophysiological measurements were continuously recorded using Acquire & Analyze software (v2.0; Physiologic Instruments).

Immunofluorescence and Microscopy
Kidneys were immersion fixed in 4% PFA/PBS for 4 hours and sectioned using a vibratome (LeicaVT1000S). Samples were permeabilized with 0.3% TritonX-100/PBS (PBS-T) and blocked with 10% donkey serum/PBS-T67. Antigen retrieval was performed with Trilogy, if needed, and tissue clearing performed using CUBIC68. MDCKII cells were fixed, permeabilized with 0.5% PBS-T and blocked with 0.7% fish skin gelatin in PBS containing 0.025% saponin (PFS)67. Tissues and cells were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4˚C, and with fluorophore-conjugated secondary antibodies for 2 hours at room temperature. Antibodies were diluted in 2% donkey serum/PBS-T for kidney sections and in PFS for MDCKII cells. See Supplementary Table 3 for antibody list.

Kidney sections were mounted in ProLong Gold. All samples were imaged with a Zeiss LSM880 confocal microscope (ZEN Black 2.3 software) or custom Axially Swept Light-sheet Microscope16. 3D projections and movies were created in Image J using the 3D projection plugin. Images were minimally processed in ImageJ (Version 2.16.0/1.54Sp) and Adobe Photoshop 2026 (27.3.1 Release), including pseudo-coloring to avoid red-green color combinations. Schematics were created in Adobe Illustrator 2026 (Version 30.1) and/or BioRender (see figure legends for details).

Urine studies
Mice were singly housed and acclimated in metabolic cages for 72 hours with food and water ad libitum. A baseline 24-hour urine sample was collected, after which the bladder was emptied and water access removed for 24 hours to obtain a water deprivation urine sample. Spot urines were collected post-deprivation. Urine osmolality was measured using an OsmoPRO micro-osmometer.

Waviness Index Quantification
3D reconstructions of ZO1-stained confocal images were generated in ImageJ using maximum projection, followed by despeckling, segmentation with MorphoLibJ, and image inversion. A convex hull was created for each cell, and the waviness index was calculated as the ratio of the convex hull perimeter to the actual plasma membrane perimeter (Supplementary Fig. 6). Dividing cells were excluded from analysis.

Statistics
All immunofluorescence analysis of mouse tissue was conducted in n ≥ 3 mice. See figure legends for panel specific details. All in vitro experiments were repeated independently at least three times. Images shown are representative. n = 9-12 mice per genotype were used for metabolic urine studies. This sample size allows detection of an effect size of 1.2-1.41 between groups with 80% power at 5% two-sided type I error. All mouse studies were analyzed using Mann-Whitney U test (for two groups) or Kruskal Wallis H test followed by Dunn’s test (> 2 groups). Waviness index measurements were compared using Kruskal-Wallis H test followed by Dunn’s test. In vitro electrophysiology data was analyzed using one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test. Graphed data are presented as mean ± s.d or in box-and-whiskers plots (see legends for details). Data was analyzed using GraphPad Prism (Version 10.3.1), with p-values<0.05 considered significant.

This study offers a straightforward and rather elegant explanation for how mammals generate highly concentrated urine for
organismal fluid balance.
Data summary: The ascending thin limb (aTL) of the nephron is long known to reside in the inner medulla, which manifests
the highest osmolality in the kidney. This study validated nephron segment-“quasi-specific” genetic lineage labeling tools to
address this question, using the Prox1-CreERT2mTmG reporter. Induction with dilute Tamoxifen concentrations allowed
visualization of lineage labeled single cell features with unprecedented clarity, revealing time-dependent development
(weeks-months) of highly branched, membrane interdigitations, resulting in a ‘sunburst-like’ cell presumably suited for ion-
transport function, given the expanded junctional seam area for these cells (Fig. 1). To understand genes/protein that drive
this morphological transition, the authors carried out single nuclear transcriptomics across post-natal development (Fig. 2),
identifying top differentially expressed genes for the aTL cluster, settling on Claudin 10 as a gene that emerges during the
temporal window when membrane interdigitation develops (Fig. 2D,E). Since Claudin 10 comes in two functionally distinct
isoforms (A,B), the authors showed it was the cation-specific 10b isoform that is expressed the aTL (Fig. 2G), consistent with
it being a candidate for sodium resorption in the kidney.
The authors turned to a reductionist claudin-null MDCK cell system to address whether Cldn10b was sufficient to drive
similar apical junction features seen in the aTL (Fig. 3; Fig. S5). MDCK tight junctions are known to display waviness in
mature monolayers, a feature previously ascribed to the claudins expressed in MDCK. Using this system, the authors
showed that Cldn10b is sufficient (in the MDCK-pan claudin-null background) to promote apical junction waviness, using
established calculation methods. Most remarkably, targeted loss of Claudin10 in mice inhibited the apical junction
waviness/interdigitation in aTL cells (Fig. 3C-F). Along with these dramatic morphological differences, the authors show
functional differences in urine osmolarity—where the Cldn10 KO mice show more dilute urine, suggestive of less capacity to
resorb sodium (Fig. 4). To further refine understanding- the authors use a panel of previously established mutants, to show
that it is the transcellular-recognition and ZO-1/ZO-2-binding domains of Cldn10, but not its ion-selective function, that is
required for the wavy/interdigitated morphology (Fig. 5).
Assessment: Overall, this is a clearly presented well designed study that links a spectacular aTL apical junction/membrane
form to kidney function/generation of concentrated urine. The notion that Cldns are regulators of epithelial membrane
structure- not simply barrier function as previously known, is compelling. I have no major concerns, but have technical
questions and minor suggestions regarding terminology (e.g., ruffling, protrusions, lateral interdigitations), which may better
align with terminology in the epithelial junction field.

rather that fully blocks the membrane elaborations? Please elaborate.
2. Is there an overall viability phenotype with the Prox-Cldn10 KO mouse?
3. For the urine osmolarity measurements in Fig. 4, did the authors use the lowest dose of TMX to bias Cldn10 removal from
the medulla, rather than other segments of the nephron?

### Reviewer 2

I would like to thank the authors for their thorough responses to the previous round of review. The revisions have
significantly improved the clarity of this important manuscript. However, upon reading the revised version of the manuscript,
additional questions have emerged that require further clarification before the manuscript is suitable for publication.

mediated translocation of the Cre recombinase to the nucleus, this is technically an inducible knockout rather than a
conditional knockout. This terminology should be corrected for technical accuracy.
2) What ages are the mice whose kidneys are shown in Figures 3c-g? Can the authors also provide more clarity regarding
the mouse ages in every figure? For instance, “adult” can indicate quite a broad age range. It would be preferred if they can
provide ages in weeks or months for each figure.
3) At what age was Cldn10 deletion induced in the mice in Figure 3? They note in Supplemental Figure 10 that deletion was
induced at P2-P7, P5-P13, and P28-P32, but they do not specify which of these deletion timepoints was used for Figure 3.
4) The authors note using mixed sex mice for each experiment – are they able to comment on whether they noted any
differences in male mice versus female mice?
5) At what age was Cldn10 expression checked in the lymphatics by immunostaining in supplemental Figure 4a? It would
be good to ensure that Cldn10 is not expressed in lymphatics at the timepoints used for all Cldn10 deletion experiments (P2-
P7, P5-P13, and P28-P32) - this will help eliminate the possibility of the phenotype resulting from off-target effects of the
Prox1-CreERT2 on the lymphatics.
This is especially important, as areas of recombination are seen as GFP expression in between tubules in Supplemental
Figure 10 (specifically in the cortex and OSOM) – these areas are presumably the lymphatics that are known to express
Prox1 as the authors point out at the beginning of the Results section. However, if Cldn10 is not expressed in the lymphatics,
Prox1-CreERT2 expression in the lymphatics should not affect the phenotype in these mice. Therefore, showing the
absence of Cldn10 expression in the lymphatics at each deletion timepoint is very important.
6) Since the same mice were used for both baseline 24 hour urine studies and the subsequent water deprivation test, can
the authors provide a graph of the change in urine osmolality between normal conditions and water deprivation for each
mouse? In Figures 4A and 4C, it looks like the urine osmolality in mutants does increase (< 2000 mOsm/kg to > 2000
mOsm/kg) after water deprivation, so they don't seem to have complete inability to concentrate urine. It would be good to see
the delta or change in urine concentration between normal and water deprivation conditions in mutants vs controls. Can the
authors also provide the urine volume in 24 hrs with the water deprivation if these data are available as well? Would expect
the volume to decrease much more significantly in the control/het mice compared to the mutants.
7) In the discussion, the authors claim that the urinary concentrating function of the aTL “is dependent on a unique
morphological adaptation” and that “this loss of claudin-10b-mediated aTL interdigitation causes a urinary concentration
defect, underscoring how intricate cell architectures enable unique physiological capabilities”.
However, I do not believe that the authors have sufficient evidence to claim that the urinary concentrating defect due to
Cldn10 deletion is a direct result of the loss of interdigitations. They have clearly shown that Cldn10b is needed for formation

sodium permeability of the cells. Thus, both the mouse model and the cell culture model provide insufficient evidence to link
the aTL’s interdigitations to its urinary concentrating ability.
